column3: It directly confirms that the messenger's recompense belongs to the Lord rather than the hearers, grounding the focus's refusal of payment.
Its unpaid proclamation is a reminder for all people, clarifying that the focus's message is not a purchased service.
The regret at not taking a path with the messenger becomes the focus's present invitation for each willing person to take a path to the Lord.
It repeats the messenger's refusal of audience payment, though the same formula has already supplied the central parallel.
The objection to a messenger who eats and walks in markets supplies local opposition to the messenger whose call is not commercial.
Its legal use of “way” concerns obligations toward others, only distantly contrasting with the freely taken path to the Lord.
It is another instance of the unpaid-messenger formula, now largely redundant after the earlier repetitions.
The possibility of a warner in every town frames the messenger's warning role, but does not explain the focus's requested response.
It rejects the claim that following another's path transfers responsibility, reinforcing the focus's personal and voluntary taking of a path.

The warning against claiming certainty about tomorrow has no clear bearing on the unpaid call or the path.

Its enduring reward for faith and good works is a different kind of recompense from the focus's rejected fee.
The denial that the Merciful should take a child does not clarify the focus.

The abundance of the gardens does not illuminate the focus's message or route.
Its assertion of God's oneness does not add a specific relation to the focus.
The question whether the audience is burdened by a fee directly reinforces the focus's refusal to impose a payment obligation.
God's dominion and witness do not specifically clarify the requested path or rejected wage.

Its warning about alliances does not clarify the focus's path to the Lord.
The immediate command to strive with the Quran supplies the active messenger task that the focus presents as unpaid and answerable by a chosen path.

God's knowledge of all things does not clarify the focus's call.
Turning from the Lord and being led from His path contrasts with the focus's invitation to take a path toward Him.

It qualifies the focus's “whoever wills”: human willing remains real while occurring only within God's will.
Its brief statement about not being able to tempt does not add a clear connection.

Measured growth in the earth does not clarify the focus.

Repentance enacted in good works is a local form of returning to God, developing the response invited in the focus.

Rules of communal affiliation and inheritance do not clarify the focus.

The statement about a small number of later people has no clear relation to the focus.

Hud refuses any payment and locates his recompense with his Creator, a direct parallel to the focus's unpaid Godward summons.
The Quran guides to what is most upright, supplying the revelatory guidance by which the focus's path is known.

The messenger's complaint that his people abandoned the Quran gives the local negative counterpart to the focus's call for a willing response.
The immediate continuation directs trust to the Ever-Living Lord, identifying the reliance that follows the focus's invitation to take His path.
The refusal to prostrate to the Merciful shows local resistance to the Lord-directed response the focus requests.

It commands following messengers who ask no payment and are rightly guided, joining non-payment directly to the route recipients should follow.
The command to turn back and submit to the Lord supplies an explicit enacted form of the focus's movement toward Him.
It commands response to the Lord before an irreversible day, sharpening the urgency of the focus's voluntary invitation.
The messenger guides to the straight path, explicitly connecting his proclamation to the divine route that the focus asks hearers to take.
The command to flee to God gives a concise directional counterpart to taking a path toward the Lord.
Its question whether the audience is burdened by a fee reinforces that divine proclamation is not a debt-producing transaction.
It addresses whoever wills to take a straight path, closely paralleling the focus's voluntary adoption of a path to the Lord.
